questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the Finish-to-Start (FtS) and Start-to-Start (StS) project dependency methodologies.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the Finish-to-Finish (FtF) and Start-to-Finish (StF) project dependency methodologies, giving an example of each.
markPoints: In FtF, tasks can run in parallel but the successor cannot complete until the predecessor is complete (e.g. network testing can't finish until cabling installation is finished). questions.explanation: Model answer: In FtF, tasks can run in parallel but the successor cannot complete until the predecessor is complete (e.g. network testing can't finish until cabling installation is finished). a microcontroller integrates a CPU, memory and I/O on one chip, uses an internal bus, and is inexpensive and straightforward

questions.prompt: What is a Digital Signal Processor (DSP) used for? Give two examples of signal types it processes.

temperature

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between RAM and ROM.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between active cooling and passive cooling.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a batch operating system and a real-time operating system (RTOS).

Windows Mobile

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a compiler and an assembler.
markPoints: A compiler converts source code into a format (usually machine code) that a computer can execute
an assembler converts assembly language (low-level code) into machine code

questions.prompt: What is the role of a debugger in code development?

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a "feature" and a "benefit" of a digital system component.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A feature is something a component has associated with its functionality, while a benefit is the outcome/result from using that component.

questions.prompt: Describe how RAID 1 (disk mirroring) works and give one advantage and one disadvantage.
markPoints: RAID 1 stores identical data on two disks for redundancy
if one drive fails the other keeps the business running (advantage), but there is slightly higher write latency because data must be written to both drives (disadvantage)

questions.prompt: Explain how RAID 5 uses striping and parity, and state its main limitation.
markPoints: RAID 5 stripes data across at least three drives with parity bits written after each save, allowing missing data to be checked/replaced and improving read performance
however it can only withstand one disk failure
questions.explanation: Model answer: RAID 5 stripes data across at least three drives with parity bits written after each save, allowing missing data to be checked/replaced and improving read performance; however it can only withstand one disk failure.

questions.prompt: Describe what RAID 10 combines and why it offers both redundancy and performance.
markPoints: RAID 10 combines disk mirroring and disk striping across at least four drives, giving data redundancy (mirroring) and increased read/write performance (striping), though it lacks parity checking and a total sub-array failure can crash the whole system
questions.explanation: Model answer: RAID 10 combines disk mirroring and disk striping across at least four drives, giving data redundancy (mirroring) and increased read/write performance (striping), though it lacks parity checking and a total sub-array failure can crash the whole system.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of Network Attached Storage (NAS) and identify one drawback.

questions.prompt: Scenario: A government research department handles vast quantities of big data. Which physical storage solution should they consider, and why?
markPoints: A SAN, because it uses block storage which can be accessed more quickly than standard file storage and supports different operating systems, suiting large-scale/big data needs (though it is expensive and requires skilled management)
questions.explanation: Model answer: A SAN, because it uses block storage which can be accessed more quickly than standard file storage and supports different operating systems, suiting large-scale/big data needs (though it is expensive and requires skilled management).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Benefits: reliability (central server keeps data available), accessibility on a global scale, manageability (centralised software), security (centrally controlled). questions.prompt: What is an SSID and what is its role in wireless connections?

access points and wireless devices must be configured with the same SSID to connect

questions.explanation: Model answer: Load balancing means the network can handle high volumes of demand by having sufficient access points, so if one is overloaded traffic is automatically directed to another access point.

questions.prompt: Describe Role Based Access Control (RBAC).

once a role is assigned, permissions and privileges are set for that user/device

easy scalability

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between DSL and fibre optic wired connections.

no unauthorised connection without a cable
more reliable/stable

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a LAN and a WAN.

a WAN covers a wide area and is made up of multiple LANs joined together (the internet is an example of a WAN)

questions.explanation: Model answer: A WLAN is essentially a LAN without cables connecting hosts and servers, using wireless technology (Wi-Fi) with radio signals instead.

questions.prompt: Explain what a PAN is and how it differs from a LAN.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A PAN is a very small network of connected devices within one building/room used by an individual or small business (e.g. via Ethernet, USB or Wirefire), whereas a LAN serves a whole building of multiple users.

questions.prompt: What is a WWAN and how does it transmit signals?

questions.explanation: Model answer: WWAN (Wireless Wide Area Network) uses mobile phone signals from mobile phone service providers, rather than radio signals, to transmit over a wide area.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between bandwidth and speed.
markPoints: Bandwidth is the capacity (volume) of data that can be transferred over a network in a given time period, while speed is the rate at which data is actually sent across the network
questions.explanation: Model answer: Bandwidth is the capacity (volume) of data that can be transferred over a network in a given time period, while speed is the rate at which data is actually sent across the network.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "latency" and identify two factors that affect it.
markPoints: Latency is the measure of time taken to transmit data from one point to another over a network, measured in milliseconds
factors affecting it include distance, transmission medium (e.g. satellite has higher latency than fibre/DSL/cable), routers, propagation delay, and storage bottlenecks
questions.explanation: Model answer: Latency is the measure of time taken to transmit data from one point to another over a network, measured in milliseconds; factors affecting it include distance, transmission medium (e.g. satellite has higher latency than fibre/DSL/cable), routers, propagation delay, and storage bottlenecks.

questions.prompt: What is a "bottleneck" in networking terms?
markPoints: A bottleneck is a limitation of data flow caused by network resources, which restricts data throughput even if bandwidth is high
questions.explanation: Model answer: A bottleneck is a limitation of data flow caused by network resources, which restricts data throughput even if bandwidth is high.

questions.prompt: Describe the client–server network model, including one advantage and one disadvantage.
markPoints: In the client–server model, clients connect to and communicate with a central server that provides services/resources
advantage: centralised control of security and access
disadvantage: if the server fails, all clients suffer disruption
questions.explanation: Model answer: In the client–server model, clients connect to and communicate with a central server that provides services/resources; advantage: centralised control of security and access; disadvantage: if the server fails, all clients suffer disruption.

questions.prompt: Explain how a thin client differs from a standard computer.
markPoints: A thin client accesses resources on a central server rather than processing locally

questions.explanation: Model answer: A thin client accesses resources on a central server rather than processing locally; it has no local storage/hard drive and runs a "thinned" version of the OS, with application servers handling most data processing.

questions.prompt: Describe the peer-to-peer (P2P) network model and explain why it can offer better performance than client–server.
markPoints: In P2P, there is no central server — each computer acts as both client and server, sharing resources directly
this results in improved performance compared to client–server networks because there's no single bottleneck server, and costs are lower
questions.explanation: Model answer: In P2P, there is no central server — each computer acts as both client and server, sharing resources directly; this results in improved performance compared to client–server networks because there's no single bottleneck server, and costs are lower.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a logical topology and a physical topology.

logical topology is the way data actually passes between devices on the network, linked to network protocols, regardless of physical layout
questions.explanation: Model answer: Physical topology is the actual physical layout of devices, cables, switches, hubs and routers; logical topology is the way data actually passes between devices on the network, linked to network protocols, regardless of physical layout.

questions.prompt: Describe a star topology and give one advantage and one disadvantage.
markPoints: In a star topology, each device connects to a central hub/switch/concentrator via a point-to-point link. Advantage: easy to troubleshoot/install and no disruption when adding/removing nodes. Disadvantage: if the hub fails, the whole network fails
questions.explanation: Model answer: In a star topology, each device connects to a central hub/switch/concentrator via a point-to-point link. Advantage: easy to troubleshoot/install and no disruption when adding/removing nodes. Disadvantage: if the hub fails, the whole network fails.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a fully connected mesh topology and a partially connected (hybrid) mesh topology.
markPoints: A fully connected mesh topology has every device with a point-to-point connection to every other device, which is impractical
a partially connected (hybrid) mesh only interconnects the most critical devices, such as mainframes
questions.explanation: Model answer: A fully connected mesh topology has every device with a point-to-point connection to every other device, which is impractical; a partially connected (hybrid) mesh only interconnects the most critical devices, such as mainframes.

questions.prompt: Describe a tree (star bus) topology and identify one advantage and one disadvantage.
markPoints: A tree (star bus) topology combines star and bus topologies, with groups of star-configured nodes connected to a linear bus backbone cable. Advantage: other nodes aren't affected if one node fails. Disadvantage: if the backbone cable fails, the whole network fails
questions.explanation: Model answer: A tree (star bus) topology combines star and bus topologies, with groups of star-configured nodes connected to a linear bus backbone cable. Advantage: other nodes aren't affected if one node fails. Disadvantage: if the backbone cable fails, the whole network fails.

questions.prompt: What is a VLAN and give two advantages of using one.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A VLAN logically separates a network (e.g. by department) into virtual networks within a larger LAN/WAN. Advantages: increased security (sensitive info isolated), decreased latency, and easier scalability/troubleshooting.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A VLAN (or a WAN with appropriate topology) would suit this, since it allows department areas to be logically separated for security and easier management while remaining connected across geographical locations; a tree or mesh topology could also be justified for connecting multiple sites.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a router and a network switch.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A router manages communication between devices and connects a network to the internet, transmitting to multiple devices/networks using IP addresses; a network switch only transmits data to the specific device it is intended for within a network, using MAC (or IP) addresses, and is not required for internet access.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a Layer 2 switch and a Layer 3 switch.

a Layer 3 switch works in the network layer and uses IP addresses, typically supporting VLANs
questions.explanation: Model answer: A Layer 2 switch uses the MAC address of connected devices and works in the data-link layer of the OSI model; a Layer 3 switch works in the network layer and uses IP addresses, typically supporting VLANs.

questions.prompt: List the seven layers of the OSI model in order, from Application to Physical.
markPoints: Application
Presentation
Session
Transport
Network
Data Link
Physical
questions.explanation: Model answer: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

questions.prompt: Explain the function of the Presentation layer of the OSI model.

questions.explanation: Model answer: The Presentation layer translates data into suitable formats for the application, supports data compression, provides security through encryption, and determines data structure.

questions.prompt: Explain the function of the Transport layer of the OSI model, including what happens when a NACK is sent.
markPoints: The Transport layer ensures reliable, error-free delivery of packets
if data is corrupted, a NACK (negative acknowledgement) is sent and retransmission is forced
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Transport layer ensures reliable, error-free delivery of packets; if data is corrupted, a NACK (negative acknowledgement) is sent and retransmission is forced.

questions.prompt: Describe the two sublayers of the Data Link layer and their roles.

which controls access to the network and permission to transmit
the MAC (Media Access Control)
which controls packet synchronisation
flow control and error checking
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Data Link layer is divided into the LLC (Logical Link Control), which controls access to the network and permission to transmit, and the MAC (Media Access Control), which controls packet synchronisation, flow control and error checking.

questions.prompt: List the four layers of the TCP/IP model.
markPoints: Application layer
(Host–host) Transport layer
Internet layer
Network access (interface) layer
questions.explanation: Model answer: Application layer, (Host–host) Transport layer, Internet layer, Network access (interface) layer.

questions.prompt: Explain two key differences between the OSI model and the TCP/IP model.
markPoints: Any two: TCP/IP has 4 layers vs OSI's 7
TCP/IP uses a horizontal/protocol-orientated approach vs OSI's vertical, functionality-based approach

questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two: TCP/IP has 4 layers vs OSI's 7; TCP/IP uses a horizontal/protocol-orientated approach vs OSI's vertical, functionality-based approach; TCP/IP combines presentation and session into its application layer and combines data link/physical into its network access layer, unlike OSI which keeps them separate.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a data packet (header, payload, trailer).

questions.explanation: Model answer: A data packet consists of a header (containing addressing/routing information such as origin/destination address, protocol, TTL, hops), a payload (the actual data being sent), and a trailer (marks the end of the packet and contains error checking such as CRC).

questions.prompt: Explain what Time to Live (TTL) means in the context of a data packet.

questions.explanation: Model answer: TTL is the amount of time or number of "hops" a packet is set to exist within a network before being discarded by a router.

questions.prompt: Explain how Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) is used for error checking in a packet's trailer.

questions.prompt: What is the role of DNS (Domain Name System)?
markPoints: DNS converts IP addresses into easily readable/memorable host names (and vice versa) so users don't need to remember numeric IP addresses
questions.explanation: Model answer: DNS converts IP addresses into easily readable/memorable host names (and vice versa) so users don't need to remember numeric IP addresses.

questions.prompt: What is SSH used for, and by whom is it commonly used?
markPoints: SSH is used to securely operate services over an unsecured network using cryptography, commonly used by network administrators to remotely access, manage and control systems and applications
questions.explanation: Model answer: SSH is used to securely operate services over an unsecured network using cryptography, commonly used by network administrators to remotely access, manage and control systems and applications.

questions.prompt: Explain what virtualisation is and describe the role of a hypervisor, host and guest.
markPoints: Virtualisation separates a single physical hardware system into multiple simulated environments/resources
a hypervisor is the software that connects to the hardware and splits it into separate environments (VMs)
the hardware is the "host" and the VMs are the "guests."
questions.explanation: Model answer: Virtualisation separates a single physical hardware system into multiple simulated environments/resources; a hypervisor is the software that connects to the hardware and splits it into separate environments (VMs); the hardware is the "host" and the VMs are the "guests."

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between desktop virtualisation and server virtualisation.
markPoints: Desktop virtualisation lets an organisation install multiple OSs on a single machine and centrally configure/update simulated desktop environments across many machines
server virtualisation partitions a server so it can perform multiple functions/serve more roles
questions.explanation: Model answer: Desktop virtualisation lets an organisation install multiple OSs on a single machine and centrally configure/update simulated desktop environments across many machines; server virtualisation partitions a server so it can perform multiple functions/serve more roles.

questions.prompt: Explain what OS virtualisation allows an organisation to do.
markPoints: OS virtualisation allows an organisation to run multiple OSs side by side (e.g. Windows and Linux), reducing hardware costs, increasing security through isolation, and reducing update time
questions.explanation: Model answer: OS virtualisation allows an organisation to run multiple OSs side by side (e.g. Windows and Linux), reducing hardware costs, increasing security through isolation, and reducing update time.

questions.prompt: Describe two key features of virtual environments (e.g. isolation, aggregation, portability).
markPoints: Any two
e.g. increased security (VM manager filters guest activity)
isolation (separate environments for guests
mitigating harmful operations)
aggregation (multiple hosts combined and presented as one virtual host)
portability (guest packaged into a movable virtual image)
continuous availability (instances can move between servers without downtime)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two, e.g. increased security (VM manager filters guest activity), isolation (separate environments for guests, mitigating harmful operations), aggregation (multiple hosts combined and presented as one virtual host), portability (guest packaged into a movable virtual image), or continuous availability (instances can move between servers without downtime).

questions.prompt: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of using virtual environments for organisations.
markPoints: Benefits: efficient use of hardware
continuous availability
simple recovery
faster setup
easier cloud migration. Drawbacks: high initial investment costs
risk to data (shared third-party hardware)
challenging scalability in the short term
reduced performance under shared resource demand
unintended server sprawl
questions.explanation: Model answer: Benefits: efficient use of hardware, continuous availability, simple recovery, faster setup, easier cloud migration. Drawbacks: high initial investment costs, risk to data (shared third-party hardware), challenging scalability in the short term, reduced performance under shared resource demand, and unintended server sprawl.

questions.prompt: What is meant by "unintended server sprawl"?
markPoints: Unintended server sprawl is where many virtual servers are quickly created (rather than reusing existing ones), leading to a server administrator managing far more servers than before, complicating operations and risking data loss if servers are forcibly terminated
questions.explanation: Model answer: Unintended server sprawl is where many virtual servers are quickly created (rather than reusing existing ones), leading to a server administrator managing far more servers than before, complicating operations and risking data loss if servers are forcibly terminated.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "cloud computing."
markPoints: Cloud computing refers to the outsourcing of IT services and infrastructure, making them accessible remotely via the internet
questions.explanation: Model answer: Cloud computing refers to the outsourcing of IT services and infrastructure, making them accessible remotely via the internet.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between a public cloud and a private cloud.
markPoints: A public cloud is used by a range of end-users (organisations to individuals) via a subscription or pay-to-use basis, usually hosted by one vendor (e.g. AWS)
a private cloud is used by a specific organisation, hosted on-site or remotely, with access restricted by a firewall the organisation manages
questions.explanation: Model answer: A public cloud is used by a range of end-users (organisations to individuals) via a subscription or pay-to-use basis, usually hosted by one vendor (e.g. AWS); a private cloud is used by a specific organisation, hosted on-site or remotely, with access restricted by a firewall the organisation manages.

questions.prompt: Explain what a community cloud is and give an example.
markPoints: A community cloud is designed for and used by a group of organisations working in a particular industry, such as the financial sector
the example given is the SWIFT banking system
questions.explanation: Model answer: A community cloud is designed for and used by a group of organisations working in a particular industry, such as the financial sector; the example given is the SWIFT banking system.

questions.prompt: Describe a hybrid cloud model.
markPoints: A hybrid cloud combines the best aspects of private and public clouds, e.g. using public cloud services for general needs while keeping a private cloud for sensitive data/services
questions.explanation: Model answer: A hybrid cloud combines the best aspects of private and public clouds, e.g. using public cloud services for general needs while keeping a private cloud for sensitive data/services.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS in terms of what the subscriber versus the service provider is responsible for.
markPoints: In IaaS, the subscriber manages applications, runtime, data, middleware and OSs while the provider manages virtualisation, servers, storage and networking. In PaaS, the subscriber manages applications and data while the provider also manages runtime, middleware and OS in addition to the IaaS elements. In SaaS, the subscriber manages only the user side while the provider manages everything else (applications, data, runtime, middleware, OS, virtualisation, servers, storage, networking)
questions.explanation: Model answer: In IaaS, the subscriber manages applications, runtime, data, middleware and OSs while the provider manages virtualisation, servers, storage and networking. In PaaS, the subscriber manages applications and data while the provider also manages runtime, middleware and OS in addition to the IaaS elements. In SaaS, the subscriber manages only the user side while the provider manages everything else (applications, data, runtime, middleware, OS, virtualisation, servers, storage, networking).

questions.prompt: Give an example provider for each of IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
markPoints: IaaS: AWS, Microsoft Azure or Oracle Cloud. PaaS: Google App Engine or Microsoft Azure. SaaS: Microsoft 365 or Google Docs
questions.explanation: Model answer: IaaS: AWS, Microsoft Azure or Oracle Cloud. PaaS: Google App Engine or Microsoft Azure. SaaS: Microsoft 365 or Google Docs.

questions.prompt: Explain what DaaS (Data as a Service) provides and how it reduces data sprawl and data silos.
markPoints: DaaS is a cloud computing model providing data management (storage, integration, processing, analytics) via the cloud/network
it reduces data sprawl (vast amounts of data) and data silos (data isolated to one department) by centralising data access
questions.explanation: Model answer: DaaS is a cloud computing model providing data management (storage, integration, processing, analytics) via the cloud/network; it reduces data sprawl (vast amounts of data) and data silos (data isolated to one department) by centralising data access.

questions.prompt: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of DaaS for organisations.
markPoints: Benefits: cross-platform transfer
automatic updating
wide accessibility
reduced risk of multiple data versions
enhanced security
reduced maintenance costs
easier scalability
supports remote working. Drawbacks: increased security breach risk over networks
time-consuming transfer of large datasets
tool compatibility limitations
compliance/legislation issues across countries
questions.explanation: Model answer: Benefits: cross-platform transfer, automatic updating, wide accessibility, reduced risk of multiple data versions, enhanced security, reduced maintenance costs, easier scalability, supports remote working. Drawbacks: increased security breach risk over networks, time-consuming transfer of large datasets, tool compatibility limitations, and compliance/legislation issues across countries.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "cloud sourcing."
markPoints: Cloud sourcing is where organisations (subscribers) outsource business processes to a third-party service provider, paying for services such as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and DaaS
questions.explanation: Model answer: Cloud sourcing is where organisations (subscribers) outsource business processes to a third-party service provider, paying for services such as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and DaaS.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "cloud portability" and why providers might restrict it.
markPoints: Cloud portability is the ability for organisations to move their applications, platforms and/or data between service providers
providers often restrict it to "lock in" subscribers, though this can also deter potential subscribers from signing up
questions.explanation: Model answer: Cloud portability is the ability for organisations to move their applications, platforms and/or data between service providers; providers often restrict it to "lock in" subscribers, though this can also deter potential subscribers from signing up.

questions.prompt: Explain what "digital resilience" means and what it involves.
markPoints: Digital resilience involves understanding and mitigating digital risks, identifying and responding to problems, and learning from experience to prevent future occurrences, while continuing to deliver products/services to stakeholders
questions.explanation: Model answer: Digital resilience involves understanding and mitigating digital risks, identifying and responding to problems, and learning from experience to prevent future occurrences, while continuing to deliver products/services to stakeholders.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "data redundancy" and describe one advantage and one disadvantage.
markPoints: Data redundancy is storing the same data in multiple locations, mainly for backup/recovery and improving reliability through comparison
the disadvantage is potential data inconsistency (e.g. if an update is made in one location but not others) and corruption risk during transfer/storage
questions.explanation: Model answer: Data redundancy is storing the same data in multiple locations, mainly for backup/recovery and improving reliability through comparison; the disadvantage is potential data inconsistency (e.g. if an update is made in one location but not others) and corruption risk during transfer/storage.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between dynamic, static and hybrid hardware redundancy.
markPoints: Dynamic hardware redundancy has only one system working at a time, with a backup started on failure
static redundancy runs systems in parallel simultaneously, comparing results via a predefined algorithm
hybrid redundancy combines dynamic and static approaches
questions.explanation: Model answer: Dynamic hardware redundancy has only one system working at a time, with a backup started on failure; static redundancy runs systems in parallel simultaneously, comparing results via a predefined algorithm; hybrid redundancy combines dynamic and static approaches.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between a hot site, a warm site and a cold site for disaster recovery.
markPoints: A hot site is a fully functioning, up-to-date replica of the business environment (equipment and data) run in parallel, expensive but allows very fast recovery
a warm site has the equipment ready but data must be restored before use
a cold site only has data (or just data centre facilities) with no equipment, is cheapest, but takes longest to get running again
questions.explanation: Model answer: A hot site is a fully functioning, up-to-date replica of the business environment (equipment and data) run in parallel, expensive but allows very fast recovery; a warm site has the equipment ready but data must be restored before use; a cold site only has data (or just data centre facilities) with no equipment, is cheapest, but takes longest to get running again.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a full backup and an incremental backup.
markPoints: A full backup backs up every file and folder on the system (time-consuming, storage-hungry, but fast/robust to restore)
an incremental backup only backs up data changed since the last backup (of any type), using less storage but being slower to restore since multiple increments may be needed
questions.explanation: Model answer: A full backup backs up every file and folder on the system (time-consuming, storage-hungry, but fast/robust to restore); an incremental backup only backs up data changed since the last backup (of any type), using less storage but being slower to restore since multiple increments may be needed.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an incremental backup and a differential backup.
markPoints: An incremental backup only backs up data changed since the last backup of any kind

a differential backup backs up all data changed since the last full backup, so it requires more storage than incremental but is easier/quicker to restore (only the last full backup plus the latest differential are needed)
questions.explanation: Model answer: An incremental backup only backs up data changed since the last backup of any kind; a differential backup backs up all data changed since the last full backup, so it requires more storage than incremental but is easier/quicker to restore (only the last full backup plus the latest differential are needed).

questions.prompt: Describe what a mirror backup includes and why it is faster to restore than other backup types.
markPoints: A mirror backup includes the entire system — data, OS, applications, configurations, preferences, booting procedures and hidden files
it is faster to restore than other backup types and produces a "clean" copy without old/outdated files
questions.explanation: Model answer: A mirror backup includes the entire system — data, OS, applications, configurations, preferences, booting procedures and hidden files; it is faster to restore than other backup types and produces a "clean" copy without old/outdated files.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "device hardening" and give two methods used to achieve it.
markPoints: Device hardening is the methods/processes used to eradicate means of attack
e.g. disabling unused network ports
strict password management
multi-factor authentication
applying security patches
removing non-essential services/programs
setting access time limits (timeouts)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Device hardening is the methods/processes used to eradicate means of attack, e.g. disabling unused network ports, strict password management, multi-factor authentication, applying security patches, removing non-essential services/programs, and setting access time limits (timeouts).

questions.prompt: Scenario: A business is deciding between a hot site and a cold site for disaster recovery. Explain the trade-offs they should consider in terms of cost and recovery speed.
markPoints: A hot site costs more but allows near-instant recovery since it's a live, up-to-date replica with data already in place

a cold site is much cheaper but has no equipment or replicated systems, so it takes much longer (requiring technical setup) before the business can resume normal operations — the choice depends on how quickly the business needs to recover versus its budget
questions.explanation: Model answer: A hot site costs more but allows near-instant recovery since it's a live, up-to-date replica with data already in place; a cold site is much cheaper but has no equipment or replicated systems, so it takes much longer (requiring technical setup) before the business can resume normal operations — the choice depends on how quickly the business needs to recover versus its budget.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between confidentiality and privacy?
markPoints: Confidentiality relates to data, while privacy relates to the individual (which can be a person, business or organisation)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Confidentiality relates to data, while privacy relates to the individual (which can be a person, business or organisation).

questions.prompt: List three types of information a typical organisation might store that needs to be kept confidential.
markPoints: employee salaries
employee perks
client lists
trade secrets
sales numbers
customer information
news about pending restructuring
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any three of: employee salaries, employee perks, client lists, trade secrets, sales numbers, customer information, news about pending restructuring.

questions.prompt: Why should employee salary and perks information be kept confidential?
markPoints: Employees carrying out the same role may be paid different salaries based on experience, qualifications and training, so this information must stay confidential to avoid disputes and to comply with legislation such as the Equality Act
questions.explanation: Model answer: Employees carrying out the same role may be paid different salaries based on experience, qualifications and training, so this information must stay confidential to avoid disputes and to comply with legislation such as the Equality Act.

questions.prompt: Who typically needs access to client list information within an organisation, and why?
markPoints: A client relationship team typically needs access, since they look after clients
other employees should not access client lists unless absolutely necessary
questions.explanation: Model answer: A client relationship team typically needs access, since they look after clients; other employees should not access client lists unless absolutely necessary.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a client list and customer information?
markPoints: A client list shows individuals or organisations/businesses that interact with the organisation, while customer information usually relates to those who buy goods or services and may include order history
questions.explanation: Model answer: A client list shows individuals or organisations/businesses that interact with the organisation, while customer information usually relates to those who buy goods or services and may include order history.

questions.prompt: Define "external stakeholders" and "internal stakeholders", giving an example of each.
markPoints: External stakeholders are groups outside an organisation, e.g. shareholders
internal stakeholders are groups within an organisation, e.g. owners and employees
questions.explanation: Model answer: External stakeholders are groups outside an organisation, e.g. shareholders; internal stakeholders are groups within an organisation, e.g. owners and employees.

questions.prompt: Why might sales numbers be relevant to shareholders or investors?
markPoints: Some organisations give financial bonuses or dividends to employees, investors or shareholders based on the previous year's sales numbers, so stakeholders may be kept informed
questions.explanation: Model answer: Some organisations give financial bonuses or dividends to employees, investors or shareholders based on the previous year's sales numbers, so stakeholders may be kept informed.

questions.prompt: What legal protection commonly applies to trade secrets relating to specific goods an organisation sells?
markPoints: Trade secrets relating to specific goods are often protected by a patent, covered under the IPA (which also covers software processes)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Trade secrets relating to specific goods are often protected by a patent, covered under the IPA (which also covers software processes).

questions.prompt: Describe one possible impact on employees if news of a pending restructuring is leaked.
markPoints: Employees may worry about losing their jobs and start looking for a different employer
customer/client confidence may also decrease
questions.explanation: Model answer: Employees may worry about losing their jobs and start looking for a different employer; customer/client confidence may also decrease.

questions.prompt: Name two methods organisations can use to maximise privacy and confidentiality of data.
markPoints: Using access controls, privileges, authorisation and other security procedures to limit access
and regularly backing up important data to a secure location
questions.explanation: Model answer: Using access controls, privileges, authorisation and other security procedures to limit access; and regularly backing up important data to a secure location.

questions.prompt: Identify two financial impacts on an organisation of failing to maintain privacy and confidentiality.
markPoints: payment of compensation
increased costs for security/new hardware and its installation/maintenance
loss of customers leading to loss of revenue
loss of revenue from lost invoices
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: payment of compensation, increased costs for security/new hardware and its installation/maintenance, loss of customers leading to loss of revenue, loss of revenue from lost invoices.

questions.prompt: Why can the timing of data backups still lead to data loss even when backups are taken regularly?
markPoints: There is always a time delay before the most recent backup can be used to reinstate data, so any data created or changed since the last backup (e.g. customer orders) can still be lost
questions.explanation: Model answer: There is always a time delay before the most recent backup can be used to reinstate data, so any data created or changed since the last backup (e.g. customer orders) can still be lost.

questions.prompt: Explain one way an attack resulting in lost customer data could affect a business's reputation.
markPoints: If data is lost during an attack, customers may no longer trust the business, reducing confidence and potentially causing them to move to a competitor, which can lead to a downturn in trading
questions.explanation: Model answer: If data is lost during an attack, customers may no longer trust the business, reducing confidence and potentially causing them to move to a competitor, which can lead to a downturn in trading.

questions.prompt: Give one example of a real-world data breach and briefly describe what happened.
markPoints: Example: In April 2017 the loan firm Wonga was attacked and the data of more than 250,000 users was stolen
or in 2008 Facebook made public the dates of birth of 80 million users
questions.explanation: Model answer: Example: In April 2017 the loan firm Wonga was attacked and the data of more than 250,000 users was stolen; or in 2008 Facebook made public the dates of birth of 80 million users.

questions.prompt: List four technical threats/vulnerabilities to systems, data and information
markPoints: botnets
DDoS
hacking
malware (including ransomware)
social engineering (pharming, phishing)
insecure APIs
use of ad hoc or open networks
eavesdropping/man-in-the-middle attacks
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any four of: botnets, DDoS, hacking, malware (including ransomware), social engineering (pharming, phishing), insecure APIs, use of ad hoc or open networks, eavesdropping/man-in-the-middle attacks.

questions.prompt: What is an API, and how can an insecure API create wider vulnerability risks?
markPoints: An API is the interface that enables two or more software applications to communicate
since data is interconnected, if one API becomes insecure it creates a vulnerability that can put everything it interacts with at higher risk
questions.explanation: Model answer: An API is the interface that enables two or more software applications to communicate; since data is interconnected, if one API becomes insecure it creates a vulnerability that can put everything it interacts with at higher risk.

questions.prompt: What is a wireless ad hoc network (WANET), and what are its two main security-related problems?
markPoints: A WANET is a network created without a wireless router or access point, where devices communicate directly with each other
its main problems are a slow data transmission rate and minimal security, making it easy for a nearby attacker to connect
questions.explanation: Model answer: A WANET is a network created without a wireless router or access point, where devices communicate directly with each other; its main problems are a slow data transmission rate and minimal security, making it easy for a nearby attacker to connect.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens during a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack.
markPoints: A hacker places themselves between two devices/users in a communication, intercepting, sending and receiving data (e.g. login or financial details) meant for someone else, without the parties knowing
questions.explanation: Model answer: A hacker places themselves between two devices/users in a communication, intercepting, sending and receiving data (e.g. login or financial details) meant for someone else, without the parties knowing.

questions.prompt: What is the "Dark Net", and how is it connected to data stolen in a MITM attack?
markPoints: The Dark Net is a network not indexed by search engines, accessible only with the right credentials
data stolen in a MITM attack (e.g. login or card details) may be posted there to be bought and used by other attackers
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Dark Net is a network not indexed by search engines, accessible only with the right credentials; data stolen in a MITM attack (e.g. login or card details) may be posted there to be bought and used by other attackers.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of vulnerability/penetration testing when a digital system is created or running?
markPoints: It identifies vulnerabilities in the system so that steps can be taken to close them before a cyber-security attack succeeds
questions.explanation: Model answer: It identifies vulnerabilities in the system so that steps can be taken to close them before a cyber-security attack succeeds.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between internal and external physical threats to digital systems.
markPoints: Internal physical threats relate to factors inside the organisation, such as system location, layout and asset robustness
external (environmental) threats relate to factors outside the organisation's control, such as natural disasters and power failure
questions.explanation: Model answer: Internal physical threats relate to factors inside the organisation, such as system location, layout and asset robustness; external (environmental) threats relate to factors outside the organisation's control, such as natural disasters and power failure.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to consider the location of digital systems in relation to fire risk?
markPoints: Digital systems should be sited away from flammable materials and have an appropriate fire alarm, but not one that automatically triggers water, since water is dangerous around electrically powered digital systems
questions.explanation: Model answer: Digital systems should be sited away from flammable materials and have an appropriate fire alarm, but not one that automatically triggers water, since water is dangerous around electrically powered digital systems.

questions.prompt: Explain how excessive humidity or dust can physically damage digital systems.
markPoints: Without proper ventilation, heat generated by digital systems can raise humidity, which can corrode or damage internal components or cause short-circuits
dust has a similarly damaging effect
questions.explanation: Model answer: Without proper ventilation, heat generated by digital systems can raise humidity, which can corrode or damage internal components or cause short-circuits; dust has a similarly damaging effect.

questions.prompt: Give two examples of poor physical access-code practices that create vulnerabilities.
markPoints: door access codes not updated regularly
using simple codes such as 1234
reusing access codes on a rotation basis
lack of monitoring of access to secure areas
unnecessary access to secure areas
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: door access codes not updated regularly, using simple codes such as 1234, reusing access codes on a rotation basis, lack of monitoring of access to secure areas, unnecessary access to secure areas.

questions.prompt: What is a legacy system, and why might a database become one?
markPoints: A legacy system is old software/hardware that has become outdated but is still in use
a database can become legacy when it needs to interact with newer software than it was designed for, forcing a decision about replacing it
questions.explanation: Model answer: A legacy system is old software/hardware that has become outdated but is still in use; a database can become legacy when it needs to interact with newer software than it was designed for, forcing a decision about replacing it.

questions.prompt: Define firmware and explain why hardware may eventually become obsolete.
markPoints: Firmware is code added at manufacture, written to a hardware device's non-volatile memory, which allows the hardware to run
hardware becomes obsolete due to reduced performance or when manufacturers/vendors stop supporting it/its firmware
questions.explanation: Model answer: Firmware is code added at manufacture, written to a hardware device's non-volatile memory, which allows the hardware to run; hardware becomes obsolete due to reduced performance or when manufacturers/vendors stop supporting it/its firmware.

questions.prompt: Explain how using an unsecured hotspot with a company laptop could create a security vulnerability.
markPoints: Using unsecured hotspots to access digital systems can leave the system vulnerable to attack, and there is also risk related to where the laptop itself is used and transported
questions.explanation: Model answer: Using unsecured hotspots to access digital systems can leave the system vulnerable to attack, and there is also risk related to where the laptop itself is used and transported.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways a natural disaster (e.g. earthquake, flood, lightning strike) could threaten digital systems and data.
markPoints: loss of internet access (making cloud data inaccessible)
destruction of digital devices/buildings/cabling infrastructure
damage to hard drive surfaces from tremors
power failure
or electrical surges from lightning strikes damaging storage devices
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: loss of internet access (making cloud data inaccessible), destruction of digital devices/buildings/cabling infrastructure, damage to hard drive surfaces from tremors, power failure, or electrical surges from lightning strikes damaging storage devices.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a malicious, a negligent and an accidental human threat.
markPoints: Malicious threats involve a conscious decision to act inappropriately with a motive to harm
negligent threats involve a conscious decision but no motive to harm
accidental threats involve no conscious decision and no motive to harm
questions.explanation: Model answer: Malicious threats involve a conscious decision to act inappropriately with a motive to harm; negligent threats involve a conscious decision but no motive to harm; accidental threats involve no conscious decision and no motive to harm.

questions.prompt: Give two examples of human error that could lead to accidental data loss.
markPoints: accidentally deleting a file or shredding the final hard copy
saving files/folders to the wrong location
sending emails with attachments to the wrong recipients
accidentally making changes to documents
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: accidentally deleting a file or shredding the final hard copy, saving files/folders to the wrong location, sending emails with attachments to the wrong recipients, accidentally making changes to documents.

questions.prompt: What is a "Turncloak" employee, and how might someone become one?
markPoints: A Turncloak is a malicious employee who uses their access details deliberately to steal information/data for financial or personal reasons, sometimes holding a grudge after being disciplined or sacked, or as a result of a social engineering attack
questions.explanation: Model answer: A Turncloak is a malicious employee who uses their access details deliberately to steal information/data for financial or personal reasons, sometimes holding a grudge after being disciplined or sacked, or as a result of a social engineering attack.

questions.prompt: Roughly what percentage of data breaches in 2019 were caused by human error?
markPoints: Approximately 90% of data breaches in 2019 were caused by human error, according to ICO/Cybsafe statistics
questions.explanation: Model answer: Approximately 90% of data breaches in 2019 were caused by human error, according to ICO/Cybsafe statistics.

questions.prompt: What does the CIA triad stand for, and what is its main purpose in cyber security?
markPoints: CIA stands for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability
its main purpose is to define and protect the important interconnected parts of cyber security for digital systems, data and information
questions.explanation: Model answer: CIA stands for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability; its main purpose is to define and protect the important interconnected parts of cyber security for digital systems, data and information.

questions.prompt: Using the online banking example, explain how confidentiality is maintained for a customer's account.
markPoints: Access-level login means that when a customer logs in, their login details only give them access to their own account and no one else's
questions.explanation: Model answer: Access-level login means that when a customer logs in, their login details only give them access to their own account and no one else's.

questions.prompt: Using the online banking example, explain what would break the "availability" part of the CIA triad.
markPoints: If the bank's website or the customer's financial records are not available when the customer wants or needs to access them, availability has been broken
questions.explanation: Model answer: If the bank's website or the customer's financial records are not available when the customer wants or needs to access them, availability has been broken.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between security, threat, vulnerability and risk management within a business context.
markPoints: Using security reduces the likelihood of identified vulnerabilities being exploited by a threat, thereby reducing risk
security must be used to maintain the CIA triad across all the interlinked components
questions.explanation: Model answer: Using security reduces the likelihood of identified vulnerabilities being exploited by a threat, thereby reducing risk; security must be used to maintain the CIA triad across all the interlinked components.

questions.prompt: What is air gapping, and what is its main advantage as a threat mitigation method?
markPoints: Air gapping is a digital system that is physically isolated (not connected physically or wirelessly) from other systems/networks
its main advantage is that, done properly, it gives complete protection with no ongoing recurring costs
questions.explanation: Model answer: Air gapping is a digital system that is physically isolated (not connected physically or wirelessly) from other systems/networks; its main advantage is that, done properly, it gives complete protection with no ongoing recurring costs.

questions.prompt: Describe how an air-gapped system could still become infected despite having no network connection.
markPoints: An infected file can be transferred via removable storage, e.g. a USB stick carrying an infected file from another network onto the air-gapped system
questions.explanation: Model answer: An infected file can be transferred via removable storage, e.g. a USB stick carrying an infected file from another network onto the air-gapped system.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between automatic and manual updating of anti-virus/anti-malware software, including one disadvantage of manual updating.
markPoints: Automatic updates check and install security patches continuously without user action, ensuring vulnerabilities are fixed quickly
manual updates rely on the user remembering to check, and can be delayed or missed entirely if the device is off when updates are scheduled, leaving the system open to attack
questions.explanation: Model answer: Automatic updates check and install security patches continuously without user action, ensuring vulnerabilities are fixed quickly; manual updates rely on the user remembering to check, and can be delayed or missed entirely if the device is off when updates are scheduled, leaving the system open to attack.

questions.prompt: Describe the three levels of API certification (private, partner, public) and state which is most and least secure.

partner certification means it's available to trusted partners
public certification means it's available to everyone (least secure)

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric (public key) encryption.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between encryption and hashing, including which one is reversible.

hashing maps data to a fixed-length hash value and is one-way/not reversible (in practice infeasible to reverse)

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a password and a passphrase, including one advantage of using a passphrase.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between logical and physical user access restrictions, giving one example of each.

physical restrictions control access to physical spaces, e.g. physical access control such as locks or badges
questions.explanation: Model answer: Logical restrictions control digital access, e.g. usernames, passwords/passphrases, data access levels/permissions; physical restrictions control access to physical spaces, e.g. physical access control such as locks or badges.

questions.prompt: Explain the four types of multi-factor authentication (possession-based, biometric, knowledge-based, location-based).
markPoints: Possession-based uses something the user has (e.g. a token/code sent to their phone)
biometric uses a physical characteristic (e.g. fingerprint, eye scan, voice)

questions.explanation: Model answer: Possession-based uses something the user has (e.g. a token/code sent to their phone); biometric uses a physical characteristic (e.g. fingerprint, eye scan, voice); knowledge-based uses agreed questions/answers (e.g. secret questions); location-based verifies the user's physical location (e.g. via wired network location or IP address/geolocation).

questions.prompt: Give one disadvantage of using biometric authentication.

questions.prompt: What is a firewall, and what is the difference between a software firewall and a physical (hardware) firewall?

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between packet filtering, proxy and inspection firewalls.
markPoints: Packet filtering firewalls analyse data packets and block those breaking predefined security rules
proxy firewalls take on the role of the intended recipient and monitor traffic at the application level (seven-layer protocols)
inspection firewalls match key features of outgoing requests against incoming traffic to decide if it is relevant
questions.explanation: Model answer: Packet filtering firewalls analyse data packets and block those breaking predefined security rules; proxy firewalls take on the role of the intended recipient and monitor traffic at the application level (seven-layer protocols); inspection firewalls match key features of outgoing requests against incoming traffic to decide if it is relevant.

questions.prompt: Explain how a password manager mitigates against threats, and identify two things it can store.

questions.prompt: Explain how a VPN mitigates against threats and what it does to a user's IP address.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A VPN creates a secure, encrypted connection to another network over the internet, masking the user's IP address so their online actions and identity are difficult to trace, and making intercepted data unreadable until it reaches its destination.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between network, social engineering and physical penetration testing.
markPoints: Network penetration testing looks for internet/external openings and vulnerabilities exploitable in the network itself
social engineering penetration testing tests human vulnerability (e.g. tricking employees into revealing login details)
physical penetration testing tests physical security measures, such as access to rooms or buildings
questions.explanation: Model answer: Network penetration testing looks for internet/external openings and vulnerabilities exploitable in the network itself; social engineering penetration testing tests human vulnerability (e.g. tricking employees into revealing login details); physical penetration testing tests physical security measures, such as access to rooms or buildings.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between white box and black box testing.
